drills.hint: Put a comma before "so", then give the result.
Cause first, then ", so" + the result clause.
"So" joins two clauses: the cause comes before it, the result after it.
Use a comma and "so" to show what happened as a result.
"So" introduces the result; "because" would reverse the meaning.
Cause, comma, "so", then the consequence.
"So" is informal but fine in essays when joining two clauses after a comma.
After the comma, "so" introduces the result.

sentences: It is banned in many offices.
drills.hint: Use a semicolon before "therefore" and a comma after it.
"Therefore" introduces a logical result after a semicolon.
Cause; therefore, result. Note the punctuation around "therefore".
Semicolon, then "therefore" with a comma, then the result.

sentences: Fossil fuels will eventually run out.
drills.hint: "Therefore" shows a conclusion drawn from the first clause.

sentences: Schools teach it from an early age.
drills.hint: The result follows "therefore,"; the cause comes before the semicolon.
"Therefore" is a sentence adverb, so it needs a semicolon before it here.
Cause first; then "; therefore," and the result.

sentences: The city built more bike lanes.
drills.hint: "Thus" is formal; use a semicolon before it and a comma after it.
"Thus" + -ing after a comma shows the result of the first action.
Semicolon, "thus" and a comma, then the result clause.
"Thus" means "as a result" and links two clauses after a semicolon.
Cause; thus, result. "Thus" is common in formal writing.
After a comma, "thus" + -ing describes the effect of the first clause.
Put "thus," after the semicolon to introduce the result.
"Thus" introduces the result; the cause comes first.
"Hence" can be followed by a noun phrase that names the result.
With a full clause, use "; hence," before the result.
"Hence" is formal and means "for this reason".
Semicolon, "hence" and a comma, then the result.

sentences: The town is near the sea.
drills.hint: After a comma, "hence" + noun phrase gives the result without a verb.

sentences: They are often tired in class.
drills.hint: Cause first; "hence," introduces what follows from it.
"Hence" shows a logical result; put a semicolon before it.

sentences: Retired people have more free time.
drills.hint: Use "; hence," to link a cause to its result.
Use a semicolon before "consequently" and a comma after it.
"Consequently" introduces the result of the first action.
Cause; consequently, effect. Keep the cause before the semicolon.

sentences: Fewer people drove into the centre.
drills.hint: "Consequently" is a formal linker for results; it follows a semicolon here.
Semicolon, "consequently" and a comma, then the result.
"Consequently" shows that the second event was caused by the first.
Put the result after "consequently,".
Cause first, then "; consequently," and the result.
Use "; as a result," between the cause and the result.
"As a result of" + noun phrase, then a comma and the result.
"As a result" introduces the effect after a semicolon.
Cause; as a result, effect. Remember the comma after the linker.

sentences: The teacher explained the rules clearly.
drills.hint: Put "as a result," after the semicolon, then the result.
"As a result of" needs a noun such as "globalisation" before the comma.
The result clause follows "as a result,".
Cause before the semicolon; result after "as a result,".

sentences: Local fishing came to an end.
drills.hint: "As a consequence" works like "as a result": semicolon before, comma after.

sentences: Many adults eat an unhealthy diet.
drills.hint: "As a consequence of" + noun phrase, then a comma.

sentences: The company moved its work online.
drills.hint: Put the effect after "as a consequence,".
Cause; as a consequence, result.
"As a consequence" is formal and introduces a result after a semicolon.
The cause comes first; the linker then introduces the effect.
Semicolon, "as a consequence" with a comma, then the result.
Use "as a consequence," to show the effect of the first clause.
"Accordingly" means "as a suitable response to this"; use a semicolon before it.
"Accordingly" introduces an action that responds to the first fact.
Semicolon, "accordingly" and a comma, then the response.
The first clause is the situation; "accordingly," shows the action taken.
Put "accordingly," after the semicolon to show the response.

sentences: The restaurant will raise its prices.
drills.hint: "Accordingly" links a situation to a sensible reaction.
Situation; accordingly, response. Keep the comma after the linker.

sentences: Some shops now open all night.
drills.hint: "Accordingly" is formal; the second clause is the result.

sentences: Water is a basic human need.
It should be affordable for all.
drills.hint: "As such" means "in that role": it refers back to the noun just named.

sentences: The old town is a historic site.
drills.hint: Use "as such" only when it refers back to a noun such as "a historic site".
"As such" = "because she is that": it points back to "a qualified nurse".

sentences: It is taught in many schools.
drills.hint: "As such" refers back to the role or category in the first clause.
"That is why" introduces the result; "that" refers to the cause.

sentences: The city has good public transport.
drills.hint: Give the cause, a semicolon, then "that is why" + the result.
No comma after "that is why": the result clause follows directly.

sentences: The flat is near the station.
It is easy to rent out.
drills.hint: Cause first; "that is why" points back to it and introduces the effect.
"That is why" is slightly informal; it follows a semicolon here.

sentences: The beach is clean and safe.
drills.hint: Put "that is why" before the result, not before the reason.

sentences: Schools include it in the timetable.
drills.hint: "That is why" + subject + verb gives the result.

sentences: Wages are higher in the city.
drills.hint: The reason comes first; "that is why" introduces the effect.
Use a comma before "which means that" to show a result of the whole idea.
"Which" refers back to the whole first clause; then add the result.
Comma, "which means that", then subject + verb.

sentences: Pupils need internet access at home.
drills.hint: "Which means that" adds a consequence of the first clause.

sentences: The park has a new playground.
drills.hint: After the comma, "which means that" + the result clause.

sentences: Drivers must take a longer route.
drills.hint: The cause comes first; "which" refers back to all of it.
"Which means that" links a fact to what follows from it.

sentences: The course is taught in English.
drills.hint: Put a comma before "which"; the result follows "means that".
Pattern: "so" + adjective + "that" + result clause.
"So" can go before an adverb too; "that" then introduces the result.
After "so" + adjective, use "that" + subject + verb for the result.
Use "so" + adjective, then "that" before the result.
"So ... that": the adjective goes between the two parts.
Formal inversion: "So" + adjective + verb + subject, then "that" + result.
Fronted "So" + adjective needs inversion: verb before subject.
Start with "So" + adjective, invert verb and subject, then add "that".

sentences: It was a very hot day.
drills.hint: Use "such" + a/an + adjective + noun, then "that".

sentences: The city has very heavy traffic.
drills.hint: "Such" + adjective + uncountable noun needs no "a".

sentences: It was a very interesting lecture.
drills.hint: "Such" comes before "a/an" + adjective + noun.
"Such" + adjective + plural noun, then "that" + result.

sentences: The region has very poor roads.
drills.hint: Use "such", not "so", when a noun follows the adjective.

sentences: It was a very successful campaign.
drills.hint: Pattern: "such" + a + adjective + noun + "that" + result.

sentences: The shop ran out of stock.
drills.hint: Formal: "Such" + "was" + noun phrase + "that" + the result.

sentences: The students had a very long holiday.
drills.hint: "Such a" + adjective + noun, then "that" + result.
